GTA 6 got off to a record-breaking start with its day-one sales, bringing in $3.79 billion by launch day thanks to 32.5 million pre-orders, but one analyst estimates its launch weekend numbers are on par with Spider-Man: Brand New Day and The Odyssey combined – and even eclipsed Taylor Swift's Eras tour. Sorry, Swifties.

Rhys Elliott of Alinea Analytics reckons that by the end of the weekend, GTA 6 had sold through a whopping 44.9 million copies across PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. Matching previous estimates from Sensor Tower, he believes that around three-quarters of those sales were on PS5 (accounting for roughly 33.7 million copies, with 11.2 million on Xbox).

To put it into perspective, the analyst says this accounts for "around 30% of the installed base per platform," so almost a third of owners of each console have bought the game.

This would place GTA 6's revenue at $4 billion in four days, Elliott says, noting that it's "roughly equal to the year’s two summer blockbusters combined (Spider-Man and The Odyssey)." Per data from Box Office Mojo, Spider-Man: Brand New Day earned over $2.5 billion from its worldwide box office revenue, while The Odyssey brought in over $1.8 billion. Combined, they're at just over $4.3 billion, so this comparison tracks – and it clearly won't take Rockstar Games long to overtake them, either, given what it's achieved in just four days.

"GTA 6 has also made twice as much as Taylor Swift's entire Eras Tour grossed across its whole run," Elliott adds. The Guardian reported in late 2024 that as of the final show of the Eras Tour, ticket revenue was at around $2.08 billion, not counting merch sales. "GTA 6 did that between Thursday and Sunday, and that's before the PC port and GTA Online," he adds.

Alinea Analytics' daily active user (DAU) estimates are also extremely strong, as you'd expect. "Our DAU estimates show that around 40.8M people logged in to play GTA 6 yesterday (Sunday Nov 22), about 76% on PS5," Elliott says. "And roughly 20% of players – almost 9M folks – have racked up over 20 hours in Leonida."

There was never any doubt that GTA 6 was going to be huge, but this really is something else. With the many, many 10/10 GTA 6 reviews, too, things really couldn't be going much better for Rockstar right now.

#3812. GTA 6 hacker pleads guilty to 2022 Rockstar Games breach which the company claim cost them $5 million

Hacker was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital

A hacker has pleaded guilty to a number of online crimes, including the 2022 breach of Rockstar Games which resulted in a bunch of mid-development clips of GTA 6 in action leaking onto the net.

The BBC report that, on November 16th, Arion Kurtaj pleaded guilty at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar Games hack and a number of others he carried out with the hacking gang Lapsus$ while aged 16 and 17. Kurtaj, now aged 21, was previously sentenced to stay in a secure hospital indefinitely due to the severity of his autism, but was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial. He'll be sentenced at a later date.

Kurtaj carried out the 2022 Rockstar hack while on bail for other hacking offences and being housed at a Travelodge hotel under police protection, the latter on account of rival hackers threatening to attack him over stolen Bitcoin stashes. The Rockstar hack was reportedly done using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into the hotel room's TV, plus a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

90 clips of unfinished GTA 6 were flung online by that hack, with Rockstar having refused to cooperate with Kurtaj's demand via an internal Slack channel that the company contact him on massaging app Telegram within 24 hours. Rockstar claimed the breach cost them $5m million to recover from, in addition to staff having to waste thousands of hours.

Earlier this year, GTA 6 suffered yet another leak, with a hacker or hackers going by "Cyberleek" posting various videos of the game in action. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two quickly sprung into action, taking down videos, filing subpoenas, and issuing a statement that called the leak "heartbreaking".

Hopefully with the game's console release later this week, those will be the only two GTA 6 leaks which have to be added to the annals of gaming history. As much as marketing can leave a bad taste in the mouth, especially when it barely shows anything of the actual product being advertised, neither of the GTA 6 leaks served much of a purpose beyond forcing people to waste some time and energy talking about the perpetrators.

#3811. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting much-requested split-screen multiplayer and new mode in 2027

The surprisingly awesome arcade podracing game Star Wars: Galactic Racer is getting split-screen multiplayer next year after loud fan requests, developer Fuse Games has announced.

Split-screen racing comes as part of an entirely new mode called Free Play that'll also allow players to mix and match vehicles, characters, tracks and planets in a galaxy far, far away. So, maybe don't expect to bring friends into the game's vast, pre-existing suite of modes just yet.

"We heard you," the studio wrote on social media. "Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at Fuse Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to Star Wars: Galactic Racer. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action."

We’ve heard you! Local split-screen multiplayer racing is coming in early 2027. A dedicated team at @Fuse_Games has been working hard to bring a brand new mode, Free Play, to STAR WARS: Galactic Racer™. This new mode will allow you to choose your vehicle, character, planet, and race track to race alone or with up to 3 other players in local split-screen action.

Galactic Racer already has a pretty good selection of online multiplayer modes, like the 12-player speeder races and 8-player podracing tours, but there's currently no way to play with your mates in the same room.

Chris Donlan loved the thrilling racing game for mixing the best bits of Star Wars and Burnout - Fuse Games does have plenty of old Criterion DNA, mind you. "It's new games, with Roguelite choices and endless unlockables, and it's also old games, with cruel and ingenious courses where everything can be lost in an instant. It's a Galaxy Far, Far Away, and it's also Paradise City," he wrote in Eurogamer's five-star review.

With Galactic Racer and Zero Company under its belt, Lucasfilm Games said it's now "more flexible" about which developers it accepts pitches from. Hopefully, that'll lead to even more interesting games set in Star Wars' ultra flexible world.

Use of generative AI in game dev remains as contentious as it does ubiquitous—a recent GDC report found that around 40% of devs use AI, but more than half think its influence has been negative. Ubisoft is continuing to double down on the technology, this time with Motherbrain, a new subsidiary fashioned from the team behind its "first playable generative AI experience."

As reported by VGC, Motherbrain's purpose is to develop "AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences … Its current focus is on new player experiences, smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large scale systemic worlds," according to an earnings report which was released Thursday.

The information comes at a turbulent time for the publishing giant, which just laid off 166 employees even after Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced "outperformed expectations." A sweeping internal overhaul earlier this year saw the company reorganize its workforce into a throng of "creative houses," a decision which led to swathes of layoffs and six project cancellations, including the Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time Remake.

It's not clear what Motherbrain are at work on, in specific terms, right now, but there may be some clues in its past work. That playable AI "experience" I mentioned earlier is none other than Teammates, an R&D project based on a prior experiment with uncanny AI "neo-NPCs."

Teammates aimed to allow players to command NPC squadmates in a rudimentary shooter game with a microphone, and using AI, have those squadmates react believably. It's not far off, at least conceptually, from what we've seen in games like Where Winds Meet and Fortnite, both of which have experimented with AI-powered NPCs.

#3808. EA really doesn't want you to delete Madden NFL 27 to make room for GTA 6

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league."

Assuming you didn't just buy a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S to play Grand Theft Auto 6, your console's limited storage space is likely already strained, meaning tough choices may have to be made to make room for Rockstar's chonky 212GB crime game.

In a move I don't remember seeing before, EA is asking players to spare Madden NFL 27 from the purge to free up console storage space. As spotted by Push Square, a desperate in-game message pops up when you launch the American Football game, pleading with you not to delete it.

The message highlights 17th November as the date of a Madden NFL 27 update, though its styling, wording and choice of background seem to hint at GTA 6.

"Don't delete!" it reads, as shared by Zirksee on X. "[Encrypted Signal] The target is locked. The crew is assembling for a high-stakes run. Await the signal from our insider on 11/17… do not leak this transmission."

EA's language and intention, however, are much clearer in this post on X, which specifically references GTA 6's large file size in a cheeky way, seemingly promoting the same update.

"Don't let 210GB get between you and your league," the post reads, clearly quoting GTA 6's file size.

The update in question is fairly notable, adding a Madden 97 throwback with era-appropriate players, playbooks and what looks to be 16-bit visuals. Though it's obviously not related to GTA 6 in any way, it's easy to see why EA would fear a significant drop in players once Rockstar's game arrives, something other publishers are undoubtedly worried about.

As part of a recent restructuring, EA laid off 400 employees, closed down BioWare, cancelled unannounced projects and revealed a refocusing on its core franchises and biggest monkey-makers. That includes EA Sports, of course, where a team is currently developing a game codenamed Project Gridiron, described as "a social-first open-world experience for our American Football team".

#3807. Intel are being sued for "misleading" investors about "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory" thanks to AI-fuelled price hikes

Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on.

All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years".

The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year.

The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen".

They also accuse the company of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above."

Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales."

Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia.

Any Intel investor who wants a piece of that lawsuit has until January 12th 2027 to sign up as a lead plaintiff – that is, a court appointee who represents the interests of other class members. As regards us little people who don't buy stock in huge technology corporations, all this merely continues the weird existential crisis wrought upon 'traditional' gaming and computing hardware by the feckless quest to sell a better chatbot.

Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzyński is going through it on behalf of all open-world game developers on social media thanks to the release of GTA 6.

In a post on Bluesky, Sarzyński says, "GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real." The Cyberpunk 2 director calls Rockstar Games' latest "probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history," citing "scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all," adding its "just a technological and creative miracle." He follows this post up with a more serious take, saying, "I think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor. GTA is impressive in a way all great art is, it expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed."

GTA 6 has inspired all sorts of praise from CD Projekt Red in general. Joint CEO Michał Nowakowski gave his congrats on launch day, while associate game director of Cyberpunk 2, Paweł Sasko, said that Rockstar has created what he calls a "generational banger."

While I don't think CD Projekt will be one of them, there will undoubtedly be a ton of investors who don't quite understand game development asking why their company can't just make its own GTA 6 and sell over 30 million copies before it even launches – similarly to that time every company was trying to make its own Fortnite. But without access to the sheer amount of time and resources that Rockstar has because it's almost guaranteed to make that money back, a game on this scale simply isn't achievable for many.

#3805. World of Warcraft: Forever's in-game economy has been ravaged by an exploit that allowed players to farm thousands of gold

World of Warcraft: Forever has suffered its first economic nightmare, as a dungeon farm exploit has left some players with thousands of gold in their bags while the vast majority of players are barely above their first hundred.

This exploit was quickly and quietly hotfixed by Blizzard, but not before a currently-unknown number of players were able to make out like bandits. In basic terms, the new Blackmaw Hold dungeon includes several packs of non-elite, easy to kill enemies right at the start of the dungeon. Prior to the hotfix, the loot drop tables for these enemies were incorrect, and worth vastly more in terms of gold than they should have. Keen-eyed players spotted this but kept it quiet, running into the dungeon and quickly killing off these early mobs and resetting the dungeon every hour.

This was possible on every class, and according to Twitch streamer Ziqo, allowed players to farm out hundreds of gold in a few hours. He is seen streaming with over 4,000 gold - and claims other streamers made out with more than that.

For an idea of how much money that is, one of the most expensive things a player will likely buy on their character throughout the original Classic World of Warcraft is the expert riding skill. It takes a long time to save up for, and stands as a major accomplishment in the life of a character. It costs around 900 gold. These players, in just a few days of dedicated grinding, will have been able to pay this price several times over.

Looking at community hubs for the game (Reddit or the official World of Warcraft forums), regular players are demanding Blizzard take action - going further than just the already-deployed hotfix. Maya on the WoW forum wants the ill-gotten gold to be removed and for players to be banned who made use of the Blackmaw Hold exploit, writing: "Remove the gold or I and many others will just quit. This is worse than the bots at this point."

Flnrodi on Reddit, referring to streamers who took advantage of this exploit, wrote: "Not sure what to say. The fact that he did this all offstream says enough that [Ziqo] (and others) knew that this is not intended and 100 percent considered an exploit. Personally, I think there should be some kind of punishment and definitely all the gold [should be] revoked."

You may be wondering why this is such a big deal? So what if a few players can get fancy mounts faster, or snatch up some really good gear on the player auction house? Well, exorbitant sums of money in the hands of a few players can have a massive impact on a server's economy. You could, for example, use your newfound wealth to flip every listing of a certain rare resource on the auction house and mark the price up significantly for profit, which obviously inflates the price for regular players. Likewise, you can out-bid other players for rare and powerful BOE items, which in turn raises the prices of those as sellers may find they can make more cash than they could off such drops prior to the exploit.

This all has an inflationary effect, and could push a server's economy to a more expensive level faster than it otherwise would. Even if this effect isn't so drastic, these players can essentially gear out multiple characters in fantastic gear without putting in the hours, or out-bid the rest of the community on the Black Market Auction House for rare and largely unparalleled special loot.

The counter argument against punitive measures is that these players didn't cheat. They didn't buy gold from real-money-traders, nor did they plug in some external tool to give them an unfair advantage over others. They simply put in the time to get to around level 55, ran a dungeon, and killed mobs repeatedly for valuable drops. Would it have been a good thing to flag the exploit the moment they found out about it? Sure. But once other players at your level take advantage of it, and no strict ruling around whether doing so is punishable, it's arguably in a player's best interest to join in while the going is good.

As of writing, there's been no official word from Blizzard on what it intends to do beyond fixing the exploit. Given the required level to take on Blackmaw Hold, the number of exploiters cannot be too large, and the sheer amount of gold they gained in a small amount of time should make them easy to flag. Rolling back their accounts and reverting the gold they gained back to a pre-exploit amount certainly appears to be a popular option. Whether Blizzard actually does so, or enforces other punishments, is the big question.

#3804. Rumour: LA Noire 2 Is Rockstar's Next Game

Okay, you'll have to stick with me for this one because it's going to take some explaining...

So, all the way back in 2023, a supposed leak on the GTAForums (please beware of potential GTA 6 spoilers if you click this link) attracted relatively little attention. At the time, there was no way to prove that any of it was legit.

The "leak" in question revealed Rockstar's schedule, with the original poster claiming that a sequel to LA Noire would be the developer's next game, after GTA 6, and it was targeting a 2030 release.

The reason it's being brought again almost three years later — chiefly via Reddit — is because as it turns out, the leaker did get a number of details about GTA 6 correct. Most notably, they managed to provide surprisingly solid info on the game's multiple endings — and they'd obviously be quite difficult to predict without some kind of insider knowledge.

To be clear, not everything in the "leak" has ended up being correct. It's a little hit and miss, but then things can change in the space of two and a half years or so; it's possible that these inaccurate details were legit at or before the time of posting.

I think the deciding factor for the believers here is that Rockstar moving on to a new LA Noire would make some sense.

Assuming it's in line with the first game, you would think that it would be a much smaller production than something like Red Dead Redemption 3 — even with the tech and engine refinements the company has made with GTA 6.

Plus, there is some LA Noire DNA in both Red Dead Redemption 2 and GTA 6; environmental and NPC interactions are key parts of Rockstar's most recent releases, and they arguably stem from LA Noire's investigative gameplay loop.

It's also worth remembering that after LA Noire's original developer Team Bondi was closed in 2011 (with Rockstar retaining the rights to LA Noire itself), its founder Brendan McNamara would go on to establish a new outfit called Video Games Deluxe.

The Australian studio crafted LA Noire: The VR Case Files years later, and even took over post-launch support for GTA: The Trilogy following its incredibly shoddy launch. Video Games Deluxe was then acquired by Rockstar in 2025, and it was renamed Rockstar Australia. Hmmm.

So some of this stuff seems to line up — but I don't think there's quite enough evidence here to nail the suspect. I mean, er, put your full trust in that original leak. Still, I wouldn't say no to another LA Noire.

Would you love to see an LA Noire sequel? Feel free to doubt all of this in the comments section below.

#3803. Each new GTA moves the series closer and closer to the original Mafia, the open-world game that bettered Rockstar

This week sees the release of Grand Theft Auto 6, the open-world crime 'em up that's been in development for at least eight years and has been waited on by fans for even longer. Naturally, over on PC we're still waiting for a port to be announced, let alone a release date to circle in our calendars. But, as happens whenever a new GTA is on the horizon, I think about Mafia: City of Lost Heaven.

Released less than a year after Grand Theft Auto 3, Mafia is perhaps a more prescient example of Rockstar's future than their own.

Set in Lost Heaven, a shoe-in for 1930s Chicago, Illinois, you play through Tommy Angelo's rise from a taxi driver, who has a chance run in with the Salieri crime family, to one of the gang's main enforcers in their fight against their rivals, the Morellos.

The influences on developers Illusion Softworks are obviously cinematic, with whole sequences ripped from The Godfather films and Goodfellas (and I'd argue there's a sprinkling of Once Upon A Time In America for good measure). A habit they share with Rockstar, who also pull liberally from crime films that share the settings of their games. But Illusion Softworks are also clearly interested in capturing the history of the Prohibition era, too. The story begins in the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street Crash and the depression that followed, running through until the late 30s, and you see that time pass in the city around you. Buildings that are under construction at the start of the game are completed by its end, a used car lot in Chinatown sits empty for most of the game until business picks up with the economy, but most enjoyable of all is that the cars driving the streets change. At first the roads are filled with Ford Model-T-inspired vehicles that basically look like horse carriages with engines, but by the end of the game they've all become much sleeker creatures that have left their early carriage influences behind.

The city Illusion Softworks built also has a dedication to verisimilitude that we see Rockstar adopting in their later games. As you drive Lost Heaven's streets, you must pay attention to speed limits and red lights, as speeding and running traffic lights will both earn you a fine if a policeman spots you. For fans of public transport, there are streetcars and overhead trams you can ride to navigate the city, too. Two other touches I love: when you reload your gun, you dump the whole clip instead of returning the unfired bullets to a magic ammo reservoir, and vehicles can run out of fuel if you drive them too far.

Much had been made of all the simulations running under the surface of Grand Theft Auto 6, such as fully realised cloud formation, a smell reaction system, and… fuel tanks that can run empty. No doubt they're significantly more impressive than what's on show in Mafia, and this isn't about putting the two games against each other (even if one of them was likely made for less than the other studio spent on coffee runs across its eight-year development). Nor is it about saying history recognised the wrong game: Grand Theft Auto 3 was a huge step forward in open-world gaming and Mafia was recognised and celebrated in its time. It's about something else.

Back in 2002, Illusion Softworks offered a different kind of open-world crime game. One that was more mature despite having a lower age rating. Grand Theft Auto was undoubtedly more influential, sparking imitators that mostly opted to follow its tone and sensibilities – Saints Row began in a similar place to GTA 3 and as the series continued leaned further into the silliness and parody, for instance. But while for many years Mafia stood as a sign to an open world path that could have been taken, the longer Grand Theft Auto series has gone on, the more Rockstar have found their way toward the example set by Illusion Softworks. The games are still aiming for bombastic comedy at times, but they're also interested in the likes of newly-arrived-in-America Niko Belic, or Michael de Santa, a retired criminal haunted by his past. They're much richer protagonists than Claude, the silent character you play in GTA 3.

The Mafia series has continued, marked by ideas that remain as interesting as what was on show in the original. In Mafia 3, you play Lincoln Clay, a black soldier returned from the war in Vietnam and brought into the family. Set in a take on New Orleans, Louisiana, during the civil rights movement, you face overt racism. Linger too long in white, wealthy neighbourhoods and the residents will call on the police to move you along. And the Definitive Edition remake of the first game, released in 2020, is a rare example of a game that both captures the spirit of the original and justifies its existence by expanding and bettering the story. Though I don't think any of its sequels have been as innovative, nor as forward thinking, as the first game.

I don't want to come across as Rockstar-bashing. The studio have continued to push the open-world genre forward with every release and I want to see what other developers lift from GTA 6 for their own games. But I'm even more pleased that as the studio's aged, their work has grown closer to Illusion Softworks'.

#3802. Sony squeezes out a PlayStation 5 firmware update before the release of GTA 6

Sony has managed to squeeze out another PlayStation 5 firmware update before the highly-anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto 6.

Sony has been rolling firmware updates out on a fairly regular basis, and like many of those updates, this latest one - version 26.07-14.23.00 - doesn't bring any very meaningful changes. Sony repeated the same "we've made some security fixes to the system software" patch-note that we've seen many times before.

And like all those firmware updates, 26.07-14.23.00 is mandatory for all PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles, assuming you want to go online or play the latest games. That, of course, includes GTA 6, which requires the console's firmware to be updated to its latest version before you can play.

The update should download automatically the next time you turn on your console, but you can also force the download through Settings > System > System Software > System Software Update and Settings. This is also where you can tick the option for your console to automatically download and install those updates in the future.

Although Sony hasn't directly said so, the high frequency of those security firmware updates is likely related to the impending release of GTA 6, especially in light of recent gen-AI-driven PS5 jailbreaks.

Any firmware released before GTA 6's release now becomes required to play the game, which delays potential security exploits, seeing as hackers would need to find vulnerabilities in that firmware in order to play. While this may never happen, Sony is at least trying to minimise the risk as much as possible.

GTA 6 arrives 19th November on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is now available to pre-load for anyone who pre-ordered the digital version, and those with the code-in-box physical version.

In a post to X, "The Everything App," US entertainment and communications conglomerate Comcast revealed that Grand Theft Auto 6's historic launch drove record-breaking internet traffic. According to Comcast, only a quarter of "the entire internet" was downloading Rockstar's latest cozy game phenomenon.

"GTA 6 didn't just break records in gaming," Comcast wrote. "Its launch drove the biggest internet traffic day in our network history, with traffic climbing 31% above an average day. At peak, GTA 6 accounted for nearly a quarter of all network traffic."

#3800. My murderous wine merchant whines for a chance at republican rule in Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion, which isn't only about the money

Longing for the Venetian Dogehouse, stuck in the Venetian doghouse

The tentacles of my trade empire snake up towards France in the west, down towards Africa in the south, and off into Hungary in the east. Yet, I still can’t reach out and grasp the throne that sits right in front of me. I’m Marco Sanudo, and the throne of the serene republic of Venice eludes me.

I’ve shed blood in its name, the blood of someone else named Marco no less. I’ve managed to avoid punishment for that crime, despite the fact it earned me a fiefdom to rule while I’ve tried to up my patrician score enough to be the lucky party the next time a ruling Doge dies in office (or runs out their 10 year term). Sadly, Doge Leonardo, the mysterious masked lord who’s had an iron grip on power since the first couple of old blokes to hold the position in this playthrough popped their clogs, is proving incredibly tough to oust.

It should, in theory, help that he’s my best mate, thanks to a well-timed feast. It certainly did in being granted a pardon for offing that other Marco, but not even that and a plague which infected nearly everyone in the realm aside from me have paved the way to Dogedom. In the meantime, I’ve striven to gain wealth and influence. I’ve worked up to having four trade routes running at once, with goods like wine, iron, and textiles flowing from market to market across southern Europe and bringing a steady supply of coin back to my Venetian estate. I’ve built trade posts at the extremities of my routes, giving me the option of starting from further afield and reaching new lands if the cash flow dries up closer to home.

This is where Crusader Kings 3’s Silk and Silver expansion has blended a bit with the game’s traditional feudal moneymaking to supercharge my coffers. The land holding I killed a dude for, the Proveditorate of Zara, means I’ve also had tax money from modern day Croatia to add to both my trade profits and the income my domicile generates on its own. I am, as the medieval kids say, minted.

Getting to the point of serious pocket clinkage is, as you might imagine given Silk and Silver’s focus on filling the game’s world with travelling merchant companies and wheeler-dealing republican patrician families, the beating heart of the expansion. A near-constant stream of notifications about prices of different goods I’m trying to hawk in different locations encourage me to regularly prune and re-work my routes so that max profits are being earned and no carrying capacity’s being wasted. The bubbling up of wars and plagues impacts prices in affected cities, making it a never-ending battle if you’re desperate to optimise everything within an inch of its life. I’ve found that degree of micromanagement unnecessary if the goal is just to keep a decent profit margin ticking over. Just remember to replace the trader assigned to a route if they die, recall them every few years so they don’t stress themselves to death, and check in every so often to re-evaluate whether you’re running goods that are suitably in demand.

If you stick at it for a decent amount of time, with a certain type of good - alcohol or jewellery, for example - your expertise in dealing in them increases, making it easier to sell for better prices. Trade routes left running between the same markets also gain boons from being in place for a long time, offering a counterpoint to rejigging them every five seconds to wring out a few more coins. Most of my routes have run along a path that includes stops at four markets, with the occasional location boasting a monopoly I’ve bargained for with the local ruler, so I don’t have to worry about competition at every stop.

When you’re playing as a merchant who isn’t locked into the ruling inner circle of a republic, making your routes as lengthy as possible is one of the three moneymaking areas your company can specialise in. That first one’s caravaneering, and is the one I leant into in a non-Marco Sanudo playthrough. Beyond that, you can become an expert loan shark, lending cash to rulers or paying their ransoms in order to recoup interest and collect hooks you can use for favours. Manufacturing expensive artifacts that can be sold individually to collectors for a profit is the third option. The latter two I’ve only dabbled in a little bit as of writing, having earned enough gold mostly from caravanneering to buy the land containing the city with my home market and be anointed a Sheikh. So, beginning as a landless merchant is a nice alternative to Crusader Kings 3’s long-established wandering adventurer starting point, with both allowing you to work your way up from lowly serf to landed lordly dynasty in your location of choice.

If you’re after a more specific historical scenario, Silk and Silver has Guelphs and Ghibellines. This is where we find Marco Sanudo, as well as the other patrician family head I’ve played as thus far, Speronella Dalesmanni. The setup is that the Pope and the Holy Roman Emperor have had a bit of a tiff, essentially rooted in who should have certain powers, with different cities and powerful families in northern Italy taking either the Guelph (Pope-likers) or Ghibelline (Holy Roman Empire-enjoyers) side depending on what suits their goals or principles. I’ll be honest, aside from being another way to easily earn friends or enemies in the ruthless crucible of merchant republican politics, where votes and reputation-bolstering aid from other nobles are key, the situation’s not had a hugely obvious bearing on my playthroughs thus far.

I think the closest it’s come is during my Dalesmanni run, if largely due to the existence of the By God Alone expansion allowing a new branch of Catholicism, dubbed Italian Christianity, to be created. The initial conversion push from the bishop responsible led a number of my fellow northern Italian nobles away from the Roman Rite headed by his Popeliness, making the Guelph/Ghibelline split more clearly defined.

In the early hours of both my Sanudo and Dalesmanni playthroughs, I’ve been far more focused on simply trying to push the respective patrician families up the hill from posh toffs with naught but a vote and a manor to elected rulers of their great cities, with land holdings to match. Speronella’s situation in Padua is made incredibly tough by the fact she’s a woman in a world where every succession rule is designed to put blokes first, so I’ve had more success with Marco and his quest to become the Doge of Venice.

As the head of a patrician family, one of select few elite clans who steer the oligarchical republic, I was faced with earning Marco enough respect among his fellow family heads that they’d consider voting him to the top of the succession list, thus securing his power whenever the current Doge got the boot. Pulling that off, while also not kowtowing to the requests and schemes of those same peers, isn’t easy. A large cocktail of factors go into determining whether another noble likes you enough to vote in support of your succession. There’s your patrician rating, which is upped by doing things which specifically show you to be good at this Italian noble house lark, such as establishing trade monopolies for the republic, gaining the Pope’s favour, or having close relatives who also hold key positions in the republic. However, how close a friendship you have with the target and how their character traits align with you also play a huge rule.

Thus it was that, at one point, Marco was best mates with the current Doge and had a decent patrician rating, but had only amassed 68 of the 72 points needed for said Doge to vote for him because the Doge was generous, and therefore didn’t care for Marco’s ambitiousness. That same Doge either liked or respected Marco enough to grant him a council position and the status of regent, but he would not back Marco to replace him permanently for love nor money. This is the same man who liked Marco so much that when I pulled off that not-so-sneaky murder on another noble house head in order to inherit the keys to the Proveditorate of Zara, the Doge was instantly willing to pardon me and prevent Marco suffering any punishment for the crime.

Not even a couple of serious plagues hitting Venice, which at one point had all three people ahead of Marco in the queue suffering from smallpox, could get him on that throne. Eventually, it took a bit of lucky timing when his Doge mate died of old age - a few years after beating smallpox - to finally install Marco as Doge. Given that delayed promotion, as of writing I’ve not yet had enough time in the big chair to give a proper verdict on how it differs from regular feudal rulerdom in the long run.

What I can do instead is tell you a bit about the fun of council votes. The same pool of voters who in a republic like Venice, get a say in who succeeds the ruler, also vote on the passage of laws and decrees. One proposal you can put forward is a vote to change who exactly is allowed a seat in this voting pool. It defaults to just being heads of patrician families, but can be extended to include all vassals, or tightened up so only the Doge’s councillors or the ruler themselves have a say, that being the way despotism lies. As you can imagine, passing a change to who can vote can drastically change the state of play, either tightening up the number of folks who might oppose or support you, or bringing new folks into play in a fashion that dilutes individual power, but gives you more pieces on the board to mind or manipulate to your advantage.

I’ve found it suitably tough to orchestrate successful votes to change laws and customs which medieval Italian noble families, expectedly, have firmly entrenched stances on. Getting rid of checks and balances, such as the requirement to vote on banishments or wars - so the Doge can rule as a despot - has proven one such challenge, as has changing laws governing men being prioritised over women. I tried to pass equal succession as a substitute for men being put first while playing as Speronella, but met an insurmountable wall of resistance due to the region’s culture and faith. So, all I could do was try to put my young male heir in the best position possible to make the sorts of gains I couldn’t.

Much easier to weasel into place, either through some canny swaying or the offering of hooks, are laws giving state backing or other priority to trading in certain types of goods. Alcohol, for instance, which certainly hasn’t hurt the profits of Marco’s two wine trade routes.

Thus, cash continues to flow through the tentacles of my trade empire in sizable globs. As he’s now Doge, I’ve got Marco using the ample funds of Venice’s treasury to build a new piazza and have him focused on making the city’s already-strong trade league even more formidable, by attracting new members from the few other northern Italian blocs.

While I’m fairly sure there are folks who’ll find Silk and Silver's constant barrage of trade route notifications annoying, or that their power-grabbing skills and sheer multitude of money-making means combine to make playthroughs less challenging than they could be, so far I've found it another enjoyably sonorous string to Crusader Kings 3’s bow. Above all else, playing as a merchant gives more reason to invest in stewardship skills beyond just maximising your tax yields, while the republican politics of the DLC's main region fleshes out rewarding intrigue-focused builds. Diplomacy and martial skills are less key, but still have their place at times.

If you’re an absolute stickler for historical accuracy, you may well find other things to gripe about, but aside from the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict fading into the background, I’ve found plenty to like in my quest to become top Doge.

#3799. After GTA 6's original soundtrack, Justice probably won't work on any other video game ever again

You've probably heard at least a little bit of the Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack from French electronic duo, Justice: a single taken from the act's original soundtrack has been released as a standalone track, and was the accompaniment to GTA 6's launch trailer. Featuring Tame Impala, SZA, and the fantastic King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard, it's clear that the duo - and Rockstar - have spared no expense on the production of music for the game.

From what we've heard so far, it's all very good: synth-drenched and poppy, a perfect mix of modern electronica and nostalgic throwback - ideal for the Miami-based setting of Vice City. You ought to enjoy the music while you can, though, because it seems Justice won't be coming back to video games any time soon. If ever.

Via a new interview with French publication Rockyrama, Justice's two members - Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay - shed a little light about their work with Rockstar, and their inspiration for joining the project. "When [the offer to work with Rockstar] arrived on the table, we thought 'if there’s one video game we have to do, it's this one.' As soon as we accepted and started working [on the OST], we thought it would probably be the first and last score we’ll ever do for a video game."

Interesting. The duo, from the clip we can see on Rockyrama's posts, don't seem to give more information about this decision - did they have a bad time working with Rockstar? Was it intense? Or is it rather down to the fact that, if you're going to work on a game, you may as well make it what is largely expected to be the biggest game of all time.

Justice, for what it's worth, consider the work they've done on GTA 6 to be "a real album" of music - it's not seen as lesser or different to the band, just because it's being released as part of a video game. "GTA 6 gave us the excuse and direction to do it. The music always had to be listenable on its own, even if each track is tailored for [a specific] scene," the band explains.

The band's album isn't the only music connected to the game, either. There's also a 34-song album launching for the game, composed of original songs from some of the biggest artists in the world. The album features Travis Scott, Rina Sawayama, Cardi B, Pinkpantheress, SZA, Keith Richards, Dua Lipa, Jennie, Lana Del Rey, Zara Larsson and many more. The full tracklist leaked at the weekend.

GTA 6 launches on Thursday, 19th November for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week

Trainer Boxes, blisters, and boosters with discounts

Buying Pokémon TCG packs can be a process fraught with risk, because of how demand has them spiralling in price. It's hard to know if you're getting a good price for a booster or bundle. That's even the case during the Black Friday sales; is a discount actually offering you a solid reduction, or is it just offering a tiny reduction from the inflated price?

That's a question I set off to solve in Walmart's Black Friday Pokémon TCG sales. The retailer has loads of pack discounts, but to varying degrees. So I looked through each one, and compared the discounted price to its actual market price, using several websites which chart this cost. Each of the 10 boosters and bundles you'll find below is now nearly at, on, or even cheaper than, its 'standard' price; these are real deals, and you can feel secure that you're actually getting a discount. They're certainly some of the better Black Friday Pokemon card deals, anyway.

This sextet of Scarlet & Violet booster packs is back down to its market price thanks to the $15 discount. That's 60 cards, for about $1 each.

Walmart has this Chaos Rising blister, featuring three boosters and a Charmeleon card, for slightly less than most other retailers thanks to this 43% discount. It also offers one of the best price-per-card deals of this list.

For some reason, Walmart has multiple listings for this Elite Trainer Box, with each sitting at a different price. This $116 bundle is the cheapest, and it matches the general market price for this set. It includes various packs including boosters, foil energy cards, sleeves, damage-counter dice and a fancy collectors'' box.

While $10 may not seem like a massive saving, again it's bringing this bundle of 6 Pitch Black booster packs to its market price. That's 6 packs for $40, undercutting some other similar packs from other series.

Another Mega Evolution six-booster bundle, but with a twist: this is about $7 cheaper than the average market price for the bundle. That makes it one of the best deals of the list, in terms of beating other costs.

This big bundle usually goes for about $118, so you're getting it at pre-inflated prices right now. The Trainer Box isn't just for booster packs, but it has energy cards, sleeves, die, condition markers and more.

The market price for this set is $124, so you're getting it at a reasonable price, although some other Trainer Boxes on this list are cheaper.

This 6-booster bundle from Destined Rivals isn't technically at market price, but only by about $2, so it's close enough to be a worthy discount. It's one of the pricier booster bundles on this list, but that still means it's much cheaper than non-discounted ones!

While this wouldn't seem like a huge saving, at 17% off, it brings the Trainer Box down to only $1 off its standard market price. If the previous Chaos Rising bundle isn't big enough for you, this is a much larger alternative.

We're looking at a discounted price that's about $6 higher than the best market price you're getting for the Trainer Box. Like others of its kind, you don't just get cards but dice and counters.

If you've been clicking through on some of these Pokémon TCG deals, you'll have noticed that some are low in stock. If there's a bundle or Trainer Box you're particularly interested in, it might be worth jumping on the discount before it sells out.

When Black Friday properly begins around November 27, we'll likely see other retailers pick up steam in the Pokémon TCG deals department — when I price checked these picks, I didn't see a huge amount of competition, but I expect that'll change soon.

However with how vast the TCG ecosystem is, there's no telling whether it'll be these exact same sets that'll see discounts. If you're just looking for a few boosters, you're probably fine waiting, but the more advanced sets may not get any discounts from other retailers. Or they may do, but not ones that sees them reach market value.

That's all to say that if these are sets you want, it's probably worth buying them. But if you had your heart set on another pack, it may be worth waiting, rather than settling for something you see here that's similar.

You'll also want to peruse our list of the best Pokémon games, and what you need to know about the upcoming Pokémon Wind and Waves. As for other tabletop recommendations, don't miss the best card games.

#3796. Spirit Crossing, the new Zelda-ish hangout MMO from the creators of Cozy Grove, understands that sometimes you just want to be alone

New multiplayer game Spirit Crossing offers up a visually blissful, but inwardly draconian world in which other people are not allowed to talk to you – indeed, not permitted access to the visible electromagnetic spectrum – unless you have given them a high five. By default, players appear to each other as shadows, all exploring a skybound landscape of magic animals and layer-cake mountains that reminds me of both Sable and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom.

Deign to slap somebody's hand, and they'll pop into colour and be able to join you for various activities. For example, going fishing, playing instruments round the campfire, playing dress-up and pulling emotes in group photos, bouncing around on strangely inflated yaks, or questing forth to heal troubled spirits. There's some material gathering and crafting, and there are recurring storms that make the ambience more threatening, but overcoming a challenge doesn't feel like the point of Spirit Crossing. The "missions" are just an excuse to hang out together.

There's nothing forcing you to do any of this in company, mind. "Stay a mysterious shadow, lend a hand when you feel like it, and disappear before anyone can make it weird," the devs explain, adding a hug emoji to make plain that they don't think you're some kind of smelly misanthrope for shunning other players.

I, personally, am a smelly misanthrope, and will only ever appear in your game as a skulking opacity, peering through the window of your personal gingerbread house, with its tastefully accessorised lava lamps and throw rugs. No, I will not join you for a group hang-glider tour. No, I do not want to play the banjo with you. You will experience me only as the nagging sensation of being watched, while you chat to the local "Stylesmith" about fetching rucksack patterns.

Spirit Crossing has an upfront cost that "gives players full access to the complete game experience in perpetuity", but you can also take out a subscription for some cosmetic items and access to a "limited resource exchange shop". They're avoiding traditional microtransactions, which is nice.

Spry Fox are also the developers of Cozy Grove - "the best grove since Byker", wrote Graham, in one of his regular 'senior moments'. I myself know them as the studio behind wintry puzzler Road Not Taken, with its randomised woodlands, and block-merging city builder Triple Town, with its unexpectedly terrifying bears. Little about Spirit Crossing seems terrifying, unless you count the shadow loitering at the edge of your conversation pit.

You can read more about the game on Steam. I find Spirit Crossing quite novel, especially when it dispenses with the WholeCosy "discover your inner fashonista" stuff and leans into the supernatural elements: I like the idea of hunkering by the campfire during a storm, watching the clouds hurtle past. Still, I'm disappointed to hear that Spry Fox have made use of generative AI during its creation.

As has been pointed out to us on Bluesky, the developers called on Anthropic's Claude tools for various behind-the-scenes tasks - the example they give in a Discord post is editing several config files at once. There's no disclosure on the game's Steam page because Spry Fox haven't used AI tools to generate any of the art or music - Valve rewrote Steam's disclosure requirements in January to exempt the usage of generative AI for "efficiency gains", which the above presumably falls under.

It's hardly a full-throated endorsement of generative AI, but it still forms part of a political and cultural project I consider reckless and morbid. For a longer account of my objections, albeit one that doesn't cover Claude in particular, here's my longform thinkywangle from July last year.

#3795. "Encouraging players to return is no mean feat" - Square Enix tempts Final Fantasy 14 players back with free game-time to fill void before new expansion

"People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons."

Final Fantasy 14 is between expansions at the moment, with Evercold preparing for release in February. So, in order to keep the game populated for the next few months, Square Enix is running a special promotion in hopes of tempting players back in.

This promotion, which began yesterday, offers players a choice between two enticing freebies. Lapsed players who haven't logged in for over six months are to be given 30 days of free game time to hop back in and catch up with the main story quest ahead of Evercold's release.

In addition, there's an alluring character skip available too. If your FF14 character is at least level 90 on one class - the current level-cap is 100 - you can skip all the way to the final part of the latest Dawntrail expansion. You still need to grind to level 100 in preparation for Evercold, but the aforementioned free month of game time should provide plenty of time to do so.

In a producer letter written to accompany this promotion, Naoki Yoshida provided insight into why this was being implemented, stating that retaining players in an MMO like FF14 was of the "utmost importance".

"Encouraging players to return is no mean feat", Yoshida wrote. "People pause their adventures for all kinds of reasons, including dissatisfaction and loss of interest. Although we continually update the game to address such issues, the fact remains that getting players to resume their journey is a difficult task indeed.

"For one, I feel that the pace of change in our lives is growing increasingly fast. Back when A Realm Reborn launched, I set policies in place based on the idea that significant changes in life usually happened in roughly three-year cycles. With that in mind, we've done our best to avoid heavy-handed attempts to secure player retention through game design, and we still maintain that philosophy even today."

Yoshida went on to explain that promotions such as this are meant as a "tiny nudge". He notes that those who have retained subscriptions continuously remain "the most important" players in the development team's eyes, and acknowledges that the process of catching up in an MMO can seem "daunting" for many.

This problem of player retention is nothing new for MMOs, especially in the tricky time between the end of a current expansion and the beginning of a new one. MMO popularity often waxes and wanes, with a new expansion acting as an exciting call to action, with the months leading up to it often serving as a natural break-point for many. Still, monthly subs pay the bills, so keeping folks around even during these quiet months is important.

Final Fantasy 14: Evercold is looking like an especially exciting expansion. On top of the new story and two classes being added, the game is getting an overhaul to combat, with both classic Reborn and Evolved action modes, as well as a new raid difficulty meant to bridge the gap between normal and savage tiers.

The game has certainly come a long way since its initial release back in 2010. Dawntrail proved divisive among fans too, though with Evercold there's a lot of hope that a new overarching storyline can bring the steal back the hearts of players old and new.

You gotta hand it to them, but the payout sounds like it would have been small potatoes to the company.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

James Lowder, a freelance writer and editor who has contracted with Wizards of the Coast on D&D books, discussed the news and its personal impact on him via LinkedIn. Here's the second half of Lowder's post, explaining the mechanics of how this came about:

"This is remarkable and amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars that WotC could have collected going to the writers. And Wizards is doing this at a time when the larger publishers are scrambling to grab as much settlement money as possible from authors. Amazing. This payout will help a lot of writers--folks who certainly deserve to be rewarded for their work.

"Conversations at Wizards about the Anthropic settlement have been ongoing for months. (I've been part of these conversations on and off, but the real heavy lifting was done by folks with more clout.) This all came about because some of the writers used what influence they possessed to raise the issue and because the people inside Wizards, up to the highest levels, were willing to consider the situation from more than a financial perspective.

"Thanks to all the writers who stepped up here. I don't think this would have happened without those author-prompted discussions, especially the efforts of R.A. Salvatore. Huge credit to the folks at Wizards, in particular Dan Ayoub, who were open to the discussions and then did the generous (and right) thing here. And it was the right thing to do."

It is unambiguously great that writers like Lowder benefitted from this settlement more than they were required to⁠—it's the spiritual opposite of all the companies that pocketed their tariff refunds instead of passing them onto the consumers who ate inflated prices. The authors who make D&D great deserve it. You do gotta hand it to Wizards.

But. In the interest of providing full context, I have to be a cynical prick for the remainder of this article. Wizards of the Coast's reputation has taken a drubbing in recent years, and even though D&D and Magic are practically synonymous with tabletop and TCGs respectively, it behooves the company to secure PR victories like this where it can.

Most recently, Wizards has refused to voluntarily recognize an employee union twice in one year, forcing a vote among the staff. The results of the ballot are not yet public, but Wargamer reported last week that the company appears to be preparing to deal with a unionised workforce.

Moving back in time, Wizards' attempt to rework D&D's influential Open Gaming License (OGL) met a huge fan and industry backlash, prompting the company to backpedal almost immediately. Contemporaneously, incidents of AI art appearing in marketing material and a D&D sourcebook similarly met with a sour response.

And the whopper: Wizards of the Coast laid off 1,100 people in 2023, including much of the publishing team that liaised with Larian Studios on Baldur's Gate 3. Larian has insisted that its decision to pivot from D&D back to its own Divinity series was a creative one, and that its shift away from Wizards was amicable, but most forum-goers and hoi polloi still assume the worst about the split.

Lowder's estimate that Wizards stood to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars here also stood out to me⁠—that's life-changing money for you, me, or even an extremely successful author like R.A. Salvatore, but it's couch cushion change for a multi-billion dollar operation like Wizards of the Coast. The real value of the case to publishers, by my reckoning, was extracting some sort of concession, a legal precedent regarding copyright and training AI models. Wizards of the Coast undeniably did the right thing here, but I think it was a PR victory cheaply bought.

#3793. Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

How an unconventional peripheral became an equally unexpected survivor

PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

Unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a new physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming."

For Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

On release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

However, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

The answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Users were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device."

In the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

"I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he says. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find new uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat."

When looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal users: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the issue of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got big as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering users.

"I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day."

#3792. Is it time to retire Dragon Quest as a series? Chrono Trigger composer Yasunori Mitsuda thinks it might be

Chrono Trigger composer Yasunori Mitsuda thinks it may be time for Square Enix to retire Dragon Quest, while reflecting on the direction of the popular RPG series after Akira Toriyama's death. The mangaka, whose art and distinct style were foundational to Chrono Trigger and Chrono Cross - and are still used in Dragon Quest to this day - died in 2024 at the age of 68.

Today, speaking via a blog post on his personal website (hat tip, Power Up Gaming), Mitsuda - a colleague of Toriyama's back in the SNES/Chrono Trigger days - suggested that maybe it's time to retire the franchise in favour of something new. This was all triggered by the announcement of Dragon Quest RPG: The Island of the Demon Tree and the Guided Island, an iOS and Android game that uses art that is very reminiscent of Toriyama's.

"The Toriyama-style illustrations for [Dragon Quest RPG] have become a hot topic, but I feel that this direction is not good for the artist, Toriyama Akira fans, and even for the late Toriyama Akira himself," said Mitsuda. "As a personal opinion, since it's impossible to create anything truly new no matter how hard you try, I feel that the Dragon Quest series should be brought to an end for now, and [Dragon Quest creator, Yuji Horii] should create a new RPG. (There have been many remakes already.)"

Horii himself seems undeterred: with the new mobile game's announcement last week, he noted that the goal of his new project is to "capture that unmistakable Dragon Quest feeling" that comes with "exploring towns, meeting new allies, gearing up and steadily growing stronger". As Mitsuda calls for the series to retire, and for something new to take its place, Horii is keen to bring "the same classic adventure" to your smartphone.

"What's important is that the game provides dreams, hope, and experiences that can only be had through games to the younger generation of children who will play it in the future," concluded Mitsuda. "But every time I see topics like this, I realise just how wonderful Dragon Quest is and how it has captivated so many people."

It's unlikely Square Enix is going to want to drop the series, of course: the Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake exceeded Square Enix's (in)famously lofty expectations, and as the company aggressively pursues its multiplatform strategy, it's hard to imagine a world in which it's going to want to move away from a series that routinely pulls in millions of sales.

While my price comparison software is saying that isn't a record low price (we did see a very brief dip to $28 last week), that's incredibly rare and seems to be a random one-off. Because this model now has a 'Black Friday deal' badge, I doubt we'll see anything better for the time being.

We've got another record low price on our hands, this time for a really sweet multi-build set that can become a fox, squirrel, or owl. It has the all-important Black Friday deal badge too, which means it shouldn't drop any further in price.

It's not the biggest price cut, but the fact that it's so darn affordable makes this a very good Lego Black Friday deal if you're tracking down gifts for a younger loved one who adores Bluey. It's never been cheaper, and has a Black Friday badge so is unlikely to drop in price any further.

Of all the Lego figures to drop in 2026, this is one of the best - we had a good time with it in our Lego Shrek, Donkey, & Puss in Boots review. The set has never been cheaper than it is now, and considering it only came out a few months ago, that's noteworthy.

Record low price? Roger roger. This kit based on Phantom Menace doesn't ever really go below $120 (with only a couple of exceptions), so seeing it hit $84 is noteworthy. If you wanted an ode to the prequels, now's your chance.

If you want a treasure trove of traditional bricks to work with either for your kids or a project you're cooking up, this is the set for you. It's not a record low price for the Black Friday Lego deals, but it is a lot better than the average cost of £32-£34.

If you're hoping to get into the Christmas spirit but also love Star Wars, I've got good news - this absolutely magnificent set has had a huge price cut. It's such a fun idea and adds a little festive flair to any setup.

OK, this is a big deal both figuratively and literally. So far as I can tell, this is a record low price and we've never seen anything better on the set since it launched in October 2026 - AKA just a month ago. It's by far the standout of the Poke-range thanks to a Polly Pocket style design that opens up to reveal a scene, so I suspect this is gonna be very popular.

One of the biggest and hottest new sets of the year just got its first ever discount, and from what I can tell, it won't go any lower for Black Friday - it's got a Black Friday badge, meaning that price should stay the same across the sale.

This delightful little set perfectly recreates the iconic DeLorean from Back to the Future, and now it's verging into impulse-purchase territory. There's a bigger version, but it's nowhere near as affordable as this... and this one still looks amazing. Plus, it's never been cheaper than it is now.

What with the final Doomsday trailer having just dropped, are there any Lego Avengers sets on offer right now? Unfortunately, none of the Doomsday-themed kits seem to be enjoying a discount - at least, not yet. I'm hopeful they will before long, because we're likely to get more official Black Friday deals on Thursday or Friday itself.

There are a lot of Star Wars Lego sets out in the wild, but a few stand out from the crowd - and as noted by our Lego R2-D2 review, the trusty astromech droid is one of them. While its discount of 20% off at Amazon US is fair, the UK equivalent is much better. It's just £54.99 at Amazon instead of £90, which brings it to a record low price.

Speaking of cute sets, another adorable one is now sitting at a record low price - the Kakamora from Moana. This kit makes two of the adorable coconut creatures, and it's been reduced to $27.99 at Amazon rather than $40 (or £25.99 at Amazon UK, down from £35). That makes this perfect giftware if you want an easy present for the Disney fan in your life.

OK, onto the discounts! Of all the Lego Pokemon sets, Eevee may be one of my favorites - as demonstrated by my five-star Lego Eevee review. It straddles the line between accuracy and functional Lego set really well, isn't so expensive it'll break the bank, and won't take ages to construct. It's currently $47.99 at Amazon rather than $60 in the US, or, for UK fans, £37.99 at Amazon instead of £55.

Can we expect to see official price cuts landing on the Lego store this Black Friday? Yes - but I'd temper expectations somewhat. While it does traditionally provide up to 40% or so off the sticker price, newer and more expensive kits aren't usually included in the roundup (with some exceptions). However, one thing it does do is offer bonus points for members of Lego's free Insiders program along with cool gifts-with-purchase. Want an advance look at what'll go up for sale ahead of the 2026 Black Friday Lego deals? You can check in with the store here.

In terms of the retailers I'd keep a close eye on, top of the list is always gonna be Amazon regardless of your region. While that may be a "well, obviously" kind of answer, it does typically enjoy the greatest variety of offers and the steepest discounts overall. It's usually matched by Walmart in the US or Very in the UK.

In terms of what you should prioritize when tracking down discounts, record low prices (identified using price-comparison software like CamelCamelCamel) are obviously the ideal situation because you know an item's never been cheaper. But when that's not possible, I'd always keep an eye on average costs. If the product in question is a lot cheaper than the batting average (as shown by price-matching sites), you should be safe to dive in.

Lego Black Friday deals seem to draw all the cheap rip-offs out of the woodwork (Amazon's listing pages become inundated with them, for instance), so be careful out there. Yes, I know - they often look amazing, seem very close to the real thing, and are a fraction of the price. But those listing images can be deceiving, and they're not always the best made. If there are enough positive user reviews then it could be worth a go, but I'd normally advise steering clear just in case you're disappointed by the result,

Before we get started, here are a few things worth bearing in mind as we delve into the discount mines in search of Lego gold. These are my guiding lights when tracking Black Friday Lego deals, so should prove useful to you too.

💲Use price comparison software: I'd highly recommend using price-matching software like CamelCamelCamel if you aren't already. These sites help you find the lowest ever price of an item, its average cost, and its history. That way you'll know if the discount you're looking at is actually a bargain or not. Not all savings are created equal, after all, so this should help you make an informed decision.

⭐ Check for 'Black Friday deal' badges: While there are hundreds of discounts floating around stores every single day, I'd be wary of hitting checkout unless the product in question has a 'Black Friday deal' badge. That means the price shouldn't change over the course of the sale, so you theoretically won't get surprised by a further discount.

I'll be leveraging all that insider knowledge so that you can secure the best bargains around, no matter what you're on the lookout for.
